L’Institut des politiques publiques (IPP) est développé dans le cadre d’un partenariat
scientiﬁque entre PSE-Ecole d’économie de Paris (PSE) et le Centre de Recherche en
Économie et Statistique (CREST). L’IPP vise à promouvoir l’analyse et l’évaluation quan-
titatives des politiques publiques en s’appuyant sur les méthodes les plus récentes de
la recherche en économie.
PSE a pour ambition de développer, au plus haut niveau inter-
national, la recherche en économie et la diffusion de ses résul-
tats. Elle rassemble une communauté de près de 140 chercheurs
et 200 doctorants, et offre des enseignements en Master, École
d’été et Executive education à la pointe de la discipline éco-
nomique. Fondée par le CNRS, l’EHESS, l’ENS, l’École des Ponts-
ParisTech, l’INRA, et l’Université Paris 1 Panthéon Sorbonne, PSE associe à son projet
des partenaires privés et institutionnels. Désormais solidement installée dans le pay-
sage académique mondial, la fondation décloisonne ce qui doit l’être pour accom-
plir son ambition d’excellence : elle associe l’université et les grandes écoles, nourrit
les échanges entre l’analyse économique et les autres sciences sociales, inscrit la re-
cherche académique dans la société, et appuie les travaux de ses équipes sur de
multiples partenariats. www.parisschoolofeconomics.eu
Le Groupe des écoles nationales d’économie et statistique
(GENES) est un établissement public d’enseignement supérieur
et de recherche. Au sein du GENES, le CREST est un centre
de recherche interdisciplinaire spécialisé en méthodes quan-
titatives appliquées aux sciences sociales regroupant des chercheurs l’ENSAE Pa-
ris, de l’ENSAI, du département d’Économie de l’École polytechnique et du CNRS.
http ://www.groupe-genes.fr/ – http ://crest.science

## 20250922-summary-Set-out-a-multi-year-tax-and-social-framework-for-the-french-industry.pdf

1

SET OUT A MULTI-YEAR
TAX AND SOCIAL
FRAMEWORK FOR THE
FRENCH INDUSTRY

Executive Summary

September 2025

2

NOTICE
This document is intended to make it easier to read and analyse the report
published by the Council of Mandatory Contributions
Only the French text of the report is binding on the Council.
Both the report and the preparatory studies are made public and can be
consulted on the website www.ccomptes.fr/CPO.

Executive Summary – Conseil des prélèvements obligatoires

3

Summary

For about fifty years, France has been facing a phenomenon of deindustrialisation,
which the public authorities have been trying to curb since the late 2000s, notably
through a policy of reducing compulsory levies on businesses. The Council of
Mandatory Contributions (Conseil des prélèvements obligatoires or CPO in French)
notes that these tax and social measures have been accompanied by a stabilisation
of industry's share of national wealth since the early 2010s, but that these tax cuts
should be maintained over time and financed in a credible manner in order to be fully
effective.

Executive Summary – Conseil des prélèvements obligatoires

4

An industrial decline exacerbated
by inconsistent tax choices

In 2023, the industry represents just
over 274,000 companies, with a
turnover
of
€1,255
billion
(bn),
generating €368 bn in added value, i.e.
14.5%
of
national
wealth,
and
employing 3.2 million employees,
i.e.15.5%
of
private
sector
employment and 12.1% of total
employment in France.
Since the 1970s, France has been
facing
a
phenomenon
of
deindustrialisation,
which
has
resulted in a decline in the share of
industry in national added value (from
25% to 15% between 1973 and 2023), a
reduction in the number of industrial
jobs (-44% over the same period), a
deterioration in the trade balance for
goods (from +€1 bn in 1973 to -€80 bn
in 2024) and in the rate of investment in
the industrial sector.
While this trend has also been
observed
in
other
European
economies, the phenomenon has
been relatively more pronounced in
France, including in the recent period:
while the share of industrial value
added in French gross domestic
product (GDP) fell by four points, from
19% to 15% between 2000 and 2023,
Germany and Poland stabilised theirs
and Spain lost three points over the
same period.
The industrial sector has strong
economic characteristics that set it
apart from services: capital intensity,
exposure to international competition,
a
higher
share
of
intermediate
consumption (such as energy), lower
sensitivity to labour costs, more skilled
and
better
paid
employment,
a
decisive role in terms of innovation and
activities spread across the entire
French territory, particularly in rural
areas and on the outskirts of cities.
The
industrial
sector
is
not
homogeneous
though:
capital
intensity is higher in the chemical,
pharmaceutical,
automotive
and
energy production and distribution
sub-sectors, the latter being the only
one with little exposure to international
competition. Salaries are higher in
coking and refining, and lower in the
food processing industry.
As defined, the industrial sector is
subject to numerous compulsory
levies of various kinds, only a
limited number of which apply
exclusively to it:
-
‘social contributions’, which
include payments made by
employers on behalf of their
employees
to
insurance
organisations (social security
1
Executive Summary – Conseil des prélèvements obligatoires

5

and other employment-related
social insurance schemes);
-
‘taxes and duties on imports’,
which are customs duties and
will be supplemented in the
future by the carbon border
adjustment
mechanism
(CBAM);
-
‘taxes on products’, which are
taxes payable per unit of goods
or
services
exchanged
(in
particular,
excise
duty
on
energy);
-
‘taxes on salaries and payroll’,
which include the mobility
payment, the contribution for
vocational
training
and
apprenticeships, the “forfait
social”
(corporate
social
contribution), etc.;
-
‘various taxes on production’,
including:
o taxes
on
land
and
buildings,
such
as
company property taxes
(notably the “cotisation
foncière
des
entreprises”
or
CFE,
which is a local tax
payable by any company
and person engaged in a
self-employed
occupation,
unless
exempted);
o taxes on other assets as
vehicles, networks, etc.,
o taxes levied on some
management
intermediate balances,
the main ones being the
business value added
tax (“cotisation sur la
valeur
ajoutée
des
entreprises” or CVAE,
which is a local tax
based on the added
value of companies with
a
turnover
exceeding
€0.5 million), and the
corporate
social
solidarity
contribution
(“contribution sociale de
solidarité des sociétés”
or C3S in French, which
is a tax contributing to
the financing of old-age
insurance, due by all
companies
with
a
turnover exceeding €19
million),
o taxes
on
pollutant
emissions resulting from
production
activities
(carbon
quotas
in
particular);
-
finally, ‘current income taxes’,
which refer to taxes levied on
profits and capital gains, in
particular corporate tax.
In total, according to CPO estimates,
excluding customs duties, the main
levies likely to weigh on industrial
companies represented a total of €91
bn for the sector in 2023.

Set out a multi-year tax and social framework for the French industry
Executive Summary – Conseil des prélèvements obligatoires

6

2

A detrimental peculiarity
of production taxation

Awareness of the phenomenon of
deindustrialisation came late, but
given its implications, particularly for
employment, the public authorities
have, since the mid-2000s, taken
measures to reduce compulsory levies
in order to counter this trend and
improve
the
competitiveness
of
businesses, which has benefited the
industrial sector.
These relief measures consisted of
reducing the taxation gap that
existed for companies between
France and its main trading partners.
This
catch-up
was
carried
out
separately for each component of the
compulsory levies structure, primarily
through reductions in the corporate tax
rate, in social security contributions
and in some production taxes.
The statutory French corporate income
tax rate (25.8%) has moved closer to
the OECD average (23.9%), which in a
context of internationalisation and
economic openness is a positive tax
signal that may influence companies'
choices regarding the location of their
economic
activities.
The
average
implicit
tax
rate
for
industrial
companies before tax credits has thus
fallen from 23.2% to 17.5%, a decrease
of 5.7 points, compared with an
average of 3.2 points for all companies.
However, this trend was reversed in the
French Finance Act for 2025 with the
creation of a one-year exceptional
contribution on the profits of large
companies.
Measures to reduce social security
contributions have helped to limit the
rise in labour costs in France and
improve competitiveness. Between
2012 and 2023, the increase in nominal
wage costs was more moderate in
France than in most other European
Union Member States. However, the
industrial sector is less exposed to
social contributions reductions than
other sectors. Indeed, on the one
hand, these reductions were primarily
designed for wages close to the
minimum wage. On the other hand, the
direct or indirect share of national
wages in French value added is lower in
industry
than
in
services.
The
extension of relief to higher wages (up
to 3.3 times the minimum wage)
benefits employees in the industrial
sector, but at these wage levels it
results in an increase in net wages
without
directly
improving
competitiveness.
The
industrial
sector's exposure to social security
contribution exemptions linked to
wage supplements varies. It is high for
profit-sharing and incentive schemes,
but more moderate for overtime. In
addition, several studies highlight the
Executive Summary – Conseil des prélèvements obligatoires

7

lack of effect of this measure on the
total number of hours worked.
France has finally made an effort to
stabilise and then reduce taxes on
production based on tax bases other
than wages. This effort focused on
property taxes, on the CVAE and, to a
lesser extent, on the C3S. However,
their level remains significantly higher
than that of main European trading
partners. Industrial companies are
particularly penalised by production
taxes for two main reasons. On the one
hand, their exposure to the CVAE
(25.9% in 2023), the C3S (29.6%) and
the CFE (24.4%) is higher than their
share of value added (14.5%). On the
other hand, some of these taxes,
particularly the C3S, have ‘cascading
effects’ on each transaction, which are
very penalising for complex and
processed goods, such as those
produced
by
companies
in
the
industrial sector.

Set out a multi-year tax and social framework for the French industry
Executive Summary – Conseil des prélèvements obligatoires

8

Place compulsory levies within
a multi-year framework conductive
to reindustrialisation

To
help
consolidate
the
reindustrialisation process, taxation
is not the main lever: the availability of
suitable land, access to transport
networks,
the
cost
of
energy,
environmental
and
social
acceptability, and the adequacy of the
local workforce in terms of quantity
and qualifications are among the key
concerns of industrial companies.
However, the tax framework remains
very important in the investment
decisions of industrial companies. Its
predictability and credibility are key to
the dynamics of reindustrialisation. It
must therefore find its place in the
French multi-year Public Finance
Planning Act which, according to the
CPO, is intended to define a multi-year
trajectory for levies by major categories
of taxes and contributions. This
trajectory should ensure, according to
a
timetable
determined
by
the
available fiscal space, the abolition of
the exceptional contribution on the
profits of large companies for those
with sales excess of €1 bn, and the
continuation of the standard corporate
tax rate at 25%, while reducing the
least efficient tax expenditures that
limit the yield of this tax (calculation at
group level of the research tax credit, or
tightening
of
territorial-based
tax
exemptions). This visibility on the
medium-term tax trajectory would
benefit companies as a whole, but
would be particularly favourable to the
industrial sector, which is more
capital-intensive and more exposed to
long investment cycles.
Beyond that, due to their direct
impact
on
industrial
competitiveness, it is important to
prioritise reducing production taxes,
depending
on
the
fiscal
space
available. In this regard, the abolition of
the C3S could be preferred to that of
the CVAE because of its damaging
knock-on effects. It could be financed
by
revisiting
tax
derogations
on
overtime schemes, that offer little
benefit to industry and have proven
windfall effects.
These last two measures would
together be almost neutral for public
finances. Depending on how the
impact
of
the
measure
on
contributions is distributed between
employees
and
employers,
the
favourable
effect
on
the
French
industry could be as much as one
billion euros (and more than four billion
for all businesses)
3
Executive Summary – Conseil des prélèvements obligatoires

9

List of recommendations

The CPO points out the dynamics of reindustrialisation depend primarily on
conditions of access to land or infrastructure, on the availability of technologies,
financing and partner companies, on the acceleration and simplification of
administrative authorisations and on the availability of adequate skills in terms of
both quantity and quality. This availability of skills can only result from better
adaptation of training to the current and future needs of industry and from the
ability of industry to retain the talent thus trained. Taxation is a means of
supporting the reindustrialisation process, but it is not the main lever. The CPO
makes five recommendations, grouped into two areas of focus.

Guideline 1: Stabilise in the long
term a tax framework that is more
conducive to French industrial
competitiveness
Recommendation 1: Set out a multi-
year framework for major categories
of taxes and contribution in the
French Public Finance Planning Act.
Recommendation 2: Incorporate
the abolition of the exceptional
contribution on the profits of large
companies into the national strategy
of fiscal consolidation.
Recommendation
3:
Partially
finance the non-renewal of the
exceptional
contribution on
the
profits
of
large
companies
by
targeting
less
efficient
tax
expenditures that limit corporate tax
revenue (calculation of research tax
credits at group level and tightening
of territorial-based exemptions, in
particular).
Guideline 2: Continue to reduce
taxes on production, prioritising
the abolition of the corporate
social
solidarity
contribution
(French C3S).
Recommendation
4:
Reduce
economic
distortion
effects
of
taxation on industry by prioritising the
abolition of the C3S over the planned
abolition of the corporate value-
added contribution (CVAE).
Recommendation 5: Abolish tax and
social security exemptions scheme
on overtime to finance C3S abolition.
The net effect of recommendations 4
and 5 would be virtually neutral for
French public finances, but would
have a favorable impact on the
industrial
sector,
potentially
amounting to up to €1 billion.
Executive Summary – Conseil des prélèvements obligatoires
